messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 55-year-old African American painter married to his longtime partner, has been struggling with the sudden and unexpected loss of his younger brother last year. The event remains vividly etched in his mind, but it is also marked by periods where he experiences intense emotions without clear images of what transpired. The trauma was triggered when John received a call that his brother had died in a car accident while driving home from work. Since then, John’s life has been irrevocably altered. The sound of an ambulance siren or the sight of emergency vehicles can send him into a state of high alert and anxiety. These triggers have become omnipresent in his daily routine, especially at his workplace where he frequently hears sirens as they pass by his studio. Each time one goes off, John’s body tenses up, and he feels on guard, unable to shake the feeling that danger is imminent. John finds it particularly difficult to feel safe at night, when the silence amplifies every unfamiliar sound. He often lies awake, listening for any noises that might signal another threat. Inside his own home, where he once felt secure, John now constantly scans his surroundings as if anticipating something bad to happen again. The grief and emotional intensity of his brother's death surface frequently, especially when he hears people discussing the loss of loved ones. These moments leave him feeling overwhelmed with sadness and a sense that his life has been irrevocably damaged. John’s negative appraisals have deepened over time. He feels like he doesn’t know himself anymore; the person he was before this tragedy seems distant now, replaced by someone who is perpetually on edge and isolated from others. This isolation only reinforces his feeling that his life has been destroyed. When John thinks about his brother’s death, he relives it through a series of vivid images—flashes of the accident scene or moments leading up to it—and these memories trigger a surge of grief and anxiety. John had come to believe that his identity was irrevocably altered by this event; his sense of self has been so fractured that he often feels set apart from others. This isolation further exacerbates his feelings of threat and vulnerability, making him hyper-vigilant in both public spaces and at home. His work as a painter has suffered because the triggers are frequent and unpredictable, causing him to lose focus or withdraw from social interactions with colleagues. What frightens John most is the thought that he might never return to the version of himself he once was. He worries about how his constant vigilance and fear will affect his relationships, particularly with his wife, who senses his growing distance but cannot fully comprehend what he is going through. Despite this, John has finally sought help out of a desire to reclaim some sense of normalcy in his life and to find ways to cope with the overwhelming emotions that continue to disrupt his daily existence. In recent months, these symptoms have become increasingly intrusive, affecting not just his mood but also his ability to function normally. The memory of his brother’s death continues to haunt him, and it is difficult for John to separate himself from the trauma that has overtaken him. He fears that he will never be able to feel safe again or find a way out of this cycle of grief and fear. John hopes that with professional support, he can begin to rebuild his life and regain some sense of control over his emotions and reactions. He is eager to learn coping strategies that might help him navigate the intense triggers that have become part of his daily experience and ultimately help him feel more connected to himself and those around him.
